items.longBusinessSummary: Amazon.com, Inc. engages in the retail sale of consumer products, advertising, and subscriptions service through online and physical stores in North America and internationally. The company operates through three segments: North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (AWS). It also manufactures and sells electronic devices, including Kindle, fire tablets, fire TVs, echo, ring, blink, and eero; and develops and produces media content. In addition, the company offers programs that enable sellers to sell their products in its stores; and programs that allow authors, independent publishers, musicians, filmmakers, Twitch streamers, skill and app developers, and others to publish and sell content. Further, it provides compute, storage, Artificial intelligence, database, analytics, machine learning, and other services, as well as advertising services through programs, such as sponsored ads, display, and video advertising. Additionally, the company offers Amazon Prime, a membership program. The company's products offered through its stores include merchandise and content purchased for resale and products offered by third-party sellers. It serves consumers, sellers, developers, enterprises, content creators, advertisers, and employees. The company was incorporated in 1994 and is headquartered in Seattle, Washington.

Title: Amazon Is Underperforming the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100. Could Oct. 29 Mark a Turning Point?
Author: Keith Noonan, The Motley Fool   Tue, October 27, 2026 at 10:15 AM GMT+1 4 min read
Published: 2026-10-27T09:15:00+00:00
=== BODY ===
While the tech giant has generally been posting impressive business results, this hasn't translated into market-beating performance for its stock. Amazon's share price has risen slightly over 7% this year, while the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 have risen 11% and 16%, respectively, in 2026.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Amazon stock's market-lagging performance isn't confined to a short-term window. Over the last five years, Amazon stock has risen roughly 49%. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 has posted a total return of 80%. Now, Amazon is gearing up to publish its third-quarter results after the market closes on Oct. 29. Does the upcoming quarterly report present a potential turning point that makes Amazon stock a buy?
Before getting into the significance of Amazon's upcoming Q3 report, it's worth exploring why the company's stock has been underperforming the S&P 500 index. While the company's leading position in the cloud infrastructure market gives it plenty of ways to benefit from the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), Amazon is posting margins far below those of other leading tech companies. This dynamic stems from the fact that the majority of the company's revenue still comes from its e-commerce business.
Amazon's online retail business is profitable, but it's relatively low-margin due to high operational costs. Meanwhile, companies including Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, and Alphabet aren't reliant on low-margin businesses for large portions of their sales -- and their stocks have played outsize roles in pushing the S&P 500 higher over the last half-decade.
Massive capital expenditures have been another source of valuation pressure for Amazon in recent years, and that trend is unlikely to change in the upcoming quarterly report. Last quarter, the company raised its capex target for the year from roughly $200 billion to roughly $220 billion. It wouldn't be shocking to see the company announce another increase to its annual capex estimate in its Q3 report.
On the other hand, this week's earnings report will likely show strong growth for AWS, solid momentum in e-commerce, and another period of impressive expansion in its high-margin digital ads business. But that also doesn't mean investors shouldn't treat a single earnings report as a catalyst to buy Amazon stock.
The good news for long-term investors is that the Q3 report doesn't need to deliver that kind of turning point. While Amazon's stock performance has lagged the S&P 500, the underlying business has generally performed very well. The cash-guzzling phase in AWS today, including the investment in custom AI chips Trainium and Graviton, has been keeping the stock down, but should reaccelerate revenue growth and lead to a free-cash-flow-generating phase over the next two to five years.
For long-term investors, I think that Amazon stock still has the makings of a strong buy-and-hold play. The company is spending massively right now, but it's investing in categories to support sales and margin expansion -- and these initiatives should pay off over the long haul.
